To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Hansen’s argument fails for several reasons.

(a) the costs of positive labeling are not as high as Hansen claims; (b) the benefits of positive labeling are greater than Hansen claims; and (c) positive labeling respects consumer autonomy more than negative labeling.

(i) Hansen underestimates the extent to which positive labeling respects consumer autonomy; (ii) she overestimates the extent of consumer demand for negative labeling; (iii) she overestmates the extent to which the cost of positive labels is borne by consumers; (iv) she overestates the cost of positive labelling, and (v) her arguments are not applicable to the U.S. context.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the extent to which labeling policies in Europe and the US respect the autonomy of consumers and citizens.
whether and to what extent the autonomy of consumers should be taken into account in decisions about labeling GM foods.
the following questions: (1) What is autonomy?

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we argue that positive labeling of GM food is not only consistent with respect for consumer autonomy but that it is also consistent with respect for the autonomy of citizens to make decisions about the kind of food system they want to live in.
the autonomy of citizens and consumers in the United States should be protected by positive labels on GM foods.

The main takeaway from our work is that
there is no good reason to prefer negative labeling to positive labeling.
in Europe, as in the US, positive labeling of GM content is the best policy option.
the European Union’s positive labeling regime is a better fit with the demands of respecting consumer and citizen autonomy than is the US regime of voluntary negative labeling.
